78.t: Different bridges instead of the I Got Rhythm changes
78.s: His originals used 32-bar choruses with altered bridges that soloists liked; he sketched routines at the piano and knew Snooky Young would phrase without markings.
78.ch: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
78.q: Oh, for blues patterns, but usually they were 32 bar choruses, which I insert little bridges to be different, a little different from the regular "I Got Rhythm" changes.

78.t: Sketching choruses and planning swing versus ballad arrangements
78.s: He sketches his chorus plan first, using about four out choruses on swing tunes and two to two and a half on ballads, varying them so they don't sound alike.
78.ch: Arranging for Fletcher, Goodman and Barnet
78.q: You know, if I was gonna make an arrangement, I'd like to set a little pattern first, you know, figure in my mind what I'm gonna do, and I'll sketch it out, you know, like what my first chorus will be, and what my next chorus, and the next. Now usually, if it's a swing thing, I'd always try to --…

14.t: His father's dance band and how he composed
14.s: Love says his father's band played dances and lancers and rags, and describes how he dreamed up pieces and had them scored.
14.q: No, he didn't have no fun with Ron. He used to play for dancers mostly. And I tell you, he had to swell all because they used to sit down and make their own music. Just make up most of the whole program, the stuff they made up. And he used to have some dancers at that time. Quadrillion and lances.…

973.t: Copyists, Richard Hayman and transposed scores
973.s: Crewe introduced him to a copyist, which led to Richard Hayman; he writes transposed scores and is transcribing All By Myself.
973.q: Yes. No at that point, at that point he introduced me to a copyist. And also a little history with the copyist, he wound up copying most of the music for the Boston Pops. Because Richard Hayman was a client of his. Later on in life I started writing arrangements for Richard Hayman, who I became…

592.t: Arranging and hearing his music played
592.s: The thrill of hearing an arrangement, and pencil-and-score-pad versus computer methods.
592.q: Oh sure. Sure. I think it’s probably what most arrangers or composers, that’s what they go for is they want to hear their music being played, especially if it comes out good you know. If it doesn’t, I don’t know what they would do, I guess they’d stop writing.

754.t: Melody first, good note theory, Schillinger and Bob Sher's reharmonization class
754.s: He writes melody first, uses good note theory, and credits Schillinger and Bob Sher's course on reharmonizing songbook tunes from ukulele changes with shaping his outlook.
754.q: Melody first. I used to write harmony first but the melodies just came out very stilted. You have to do melody first. Once you’ve got the melody then I use something called good note theory, you know, which is: is this note going to be a natural 9 or a flat 9 or is it going to be a fifth of a…

964.t: Hearing your first charts played and the Synclavier
964.s: The cringe moment of hearing a score played; Gold uses a Synclavier to sketch arrangements.
964.q: Well especially in the '70s and the '80s before we had all these computers. Now I can do a little dubbing, I have a Synclavier so I can put the song in my Synclavier and do a little sketch and I can listen to it. It's not the same at all but at least I can hear — I can play with the voicing. I can…

1036.t: Using Finale and not trusting playback
1036.s: He uses Finale for extracting parts but writes faster by hand, and told students not to trust playback.
1036.q: Yeah I use Finale only because I can extract the parts. I hate copying parts. I can write faster with a score pad and pencil. I think Gordon Goodwin can as well and Mark Taylor as well. But after you’ve got the sketch done, for me now once I’ve got it in my head I just put it down in the computer…

522.t: Finale and the Christmas Waltz shout chorus
522.s: Using Finale, and writing a Sir Duke style shout chorus the band played with little rehearsal.
522.q: Or to the players. I remember not that long ago the “Family Holidays” CD that we did has a track called “The Christmas Waltz.” Well I decided to write a kind of Stevie

965.t: From pencil and paper to Sibelius and sketches
965.s: He misses pencil scores; now he sketches on six staves, types into Sibelius, delivers PDFs and discards the sketches.
965.q: I do miss them a lot. Excuse me one second. I just happen to have some right here. Sturdy staff paper. Yes. The process has changed and I’m not real happy about it. It used to be always pencil and paper, finish it, fold it in half, put the title and the date on it, and send it away to somebody, to…

1012.s: His father wrote everything by hand in pencil, knew transpositions, and was neat, in contrast to Gil Evans per Creed Taylor on Impulse.
1012.q: These little Scripto mechanical pencils that you would — he had a million of them and he’d use those all the time. And it’s funny I still have some of the old manuscript paper. You can’t even find the stuff anymore.

585.t: Struggling without goals or deadlines; recording projects and arrangements
585.s: She says she does not work well without deadlines; Arbors and Venus Records asked for projects, and Monk mentions writing for his sax ensemble.
585.q: It’s crazy, isn’t it? I mean I’m mad at myself that I don’t have a great music library all set up. I don’t. It was one of the goals, and I have to get to it. You know what I mean? There’s certain things you have to do. You kind of have piles of music around forever and think that you can be…

751.t: Pencil scores versus Finale and Dorico
751.s: Rowe prefers writing in pencil, as Ray Wright taught; with Finale discontinued she plans to learn Dorico; Monk cites Dave Rivello.
751.q: Oh boy you’re asking such great questions. Yeah I have a million pencil scores lying around here I could hold up as my prop. Yeah I’m something of a — I don’t want to say — I’m not a troglodyte, maybe a Luddite is a better word. I grew up of a similar generation to Mike Holober and Maria Schneider…

487.t: Copying parts, pencil and paper, writing transposed scores
487.s: He no longer copies his parts, has no notation software, and writes transposed, a habit from Bobby Porcelli in 1958.
487.q: At first I did. But I reached a certain point at which it drove me crazy and I said once I finish it the way I do an arrangement is I do the whole arrangement. Then I go back to the very top and go through it again checking every little thing. After that I don’t want to see those notes for a little…

328.t: Sophisticated Giant and writing for three horns
328.s: He prefers Copenhagen; writing for three horns is harder, learned from Blakey.
328.ch: Europe years and the return home
328.q: I like the Copenhagen better, because it was my input into Sophisticated Giant that took some of the gloss off of it for me. I didn’t like what I wrote in it. I almost got to where I wanted to go, but I didn’t. Maybe it was that I was writing too fast or something. These arrangements in Day in…
